It was assumed that the mass transfer rate is proportional to the log mean CO pressure difference (LMPD) of the air side for cross-flow conditions. 2 Also, aqueous CO concentration in solution was assumed negligible due to high rate of reaction in solution 2 phase. LMPD was modified for the negligible aqueous CO concentration in the solution. Two-film mass- 2 transfer models (Onda and BRF) were finalized based on the number of parameters for estimating the CO absorption rate. The BRF model needed less model tuning in comparison with the Onda model for the 2 validation and the BRF model was in excellent agreement with the measured data. Task 5.1 In subtask 5.1, a vacuum-assisted desorption testing apparatus was designed and experiments were conducted with the goal of reducing the BIG desorption temperature below 95°C and thus reduce sensible heat requirements of the process. It is hypothesized that performing the reaction under a vacuum will reduce the temperature necessary to perform the desorption step. A combination of reducing the boiling point of the contained water (approximately 60°C at 0.2 atm(a)) and decreasing partial pressures of CO and water 2 around the sorbent was thought to allow for the desorption process to proceed at significantly lower temperatures. To run these experiments, a small test bench was designed and assembled which could operate at precisely controlled temperatures under vacuum conditions. With this apparatus, temperatures and pressures were varied to determine if the introduction of a vacuum (i) reduces temperature requirement to regenerate the BIG carbonate, and (ii) significantly improves the regeneration rate. Two different BIG compounds were tested with this apparatus. For one, near-complete CO desorption 2 was achieved at temperatures as low as 90 °C exceeding the success criteria of reducing the regeneration temperature to below 95°C. However, the results also showed that vacuum has almost no impact on the regeneration process – meaning no impact on required regeneration temperature. Overall, the findings highlight the distinct desorption characteristics of different BIGs, emphasizing the importance of tailored conditions to optimize the regeneration performance of different guanidines.
